Browsers are runtimes and webpages are apps. They just happen to be apps that are dynamically fetched over the network and are packaged as HTML/CSS/JS instead of as PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries.Runtimes can have bugs or inefficiencies that cause them to use more memory than strictly necessary, but by and large most memory problems are the product of the apps (or webpages) themselves.reply

The view of web pages as apps and browsers as runtime environments/OSes is reasonable but in my opinion it even reinforces the idea that it should be the browser duty to contain bad behavior from web apps/pages. Browsers are well positioned to do so, as they know exactly which resources are used by each tab , and how those grow over time. Also browsers already treat web content as untrusted (sandboxing, isolation), so it would be a natural next step to extend that approach to resource usage. It would match how Operating Systems work, where it's the OS acting as an "arbiter", not the userland application.reply

title: Arctic: A Practical Lock-Free Adaptive Radix Tree (usenix.org)
comments: xxx
first_paragraph: Newton Ni, Nicolas Garza, Jenny Stinehour, and Michael Goppert, The University of Texas at Austin; Michal Friedman, ETH Zürich; Emmett Witchel, The University of Texas at AustinIndexing data structures are vital to the modern systems ecosystem, but there are no indexes that offer high performance, lock freedom, and range scans. Arctic is a lock-free adaptive radix tree that achieves all three: Arctic outcompetes lock-based indexes, including a concurrent hash map, on many YCSB configurations, guarantees non-blocking operation through careful metadata layout and an (eponymous) freezing-based coordination protocol, and offers non-linearizable range and prefix scans. Arctic also contributes a novel safe memory reclamation scheme that uses operation keys to approximate reachable pointers. We integrate Arctic into RocksDB and Turso, improving throughput up to 40% and 12% on their write-heavy benchmarks relative to their default skiplist indexes.OSDI '26 Open Access Sponsored byKing Abdullah

It's my dream setup now:  A single stock remote control that controls everything with Debian in the middle.The trick was setting it automatically boot to HDMI1 so I never have to deal with ads or the slow UI.  HDMI1 is connected directly to a mini ITX case running bare Kodi with no window manager.I paired the remote with that machine instead of the TV.  And then configured it to either forward the button presses to Kodi (if focused) or forward them back to the television via wifi (which you can do via Fire TV's "developer mode").reply

IOW, the TV is a dumb display, and all smarts are in the external Linux box you control.This is completely fine. But it would be extra nice to gain control over the internal computer that also runs Linux, or at least could. It's already built in and paid for, it's just programmed in an adversarial way.reply
Agree, but one of my main gripes is how underpowered the internal chip is.  Maybe with root access one could squeeze out an acceptable level of performance.reply

This is such a cool little tinker project.
I solved a similar problem by just having an old laptop permanently running behind the tv with it's battery removed.reply

Call me old fashioned but our whole family just uses Remote on our iOS devices to control the TVs via CEC.No TV spyware (it never has network), no remotes to lose or break, no AAA batteries to change. Take advantage of what you already have in your pocket and charged at all times. Simple.(Bonus being it works over the network and not IR so you can be anywhere and control any TV)reply

The main issue (at least for me) with using smartphones / any touch screens as remote is the loss of muscle memory.. You'd have to look at the phone screen to change anything. Not to mention, having to unlock your phone, open the app etc..Once you get used to blindly reaching a button on the remote to perform an action, it would be very hard to go back.reply

I would have thought so, but for us that is not the case. I can open it in the dark and swipe. Face unlock is instant and the swiping gestures don’t require precision. I have muscle memory of the presses required to turn off the TV via CEC in another room without seeing the OSD.And if anyone claims it’s too “advanced”, my youngest has had no problems controlling any room from his iPad since at least age 6, if not earlier.You could always have a dedicated iPad as a remote instead of using a phone. The point being it’s much harder to lose an iPad on the couch than a small stick remote that finds every excuse to inexplicably disappear when needed most.The benefits of centralizing everything onto a phone that is already in the “critical path” outweigh everything else for me.reply
Maybe you can use CEC through your TV to PC for simple controls (although it may be not enough opcodes for detailed control)reply

For "Steam Deck" / "Gaming Console" Kind of use cases, CEC goes surprisingly a long way.Earlier this year I set up a BC-250 as my primary gaming console. CEC working on it was a really nice bonus I'd say. The comfort it gives me to just shut it down from TV remote.. or powering up the tv and switching to the correct source when turning it on.. it is very nice to just have a single remote to control those two devices.reply
Most PC gpus don’t have CEC at all afaik.reply

title: "Dario is hyping the dangers so OSS models are illegal and he stays in control" (twitter.com/ylecun)
comments: I work with and am friends with people who are in the regulatory space that would intersect with AI.There are some interesting conversations about how'd you ban open weight models and so far the emerging consensus is that if you can't ban the bullets, then you ban the guns. Ideas floated range from requiring companies like AMD and Nvidia to push microcode updates that limit consumer grade GPUs abilities to work with LLMs, to require some kind of registration for privately owned compute, to even just requiring that GPUs are just outright surrendered.It sounds crazy, but then I was pointed to Executed Order 6102 which is the Gold Confiscation act by FDR and opens a pathway to some kind of asset seizure. I think a lof of those in the "AI Safety-ist" camp realize that the toothpaste is out of the tube and that something that feels "draconian" in the name of state security may be needed.reply

>There are some interesting conversations about how'd you ban open weight models and so far the emerging consensus is that if you can't ban the bullets, then you ban the guns.Or you could just impose tort liability for individuals who misuse models, OSS or otherwise, and not ban anything.I've never figured out why nearly all of the air in the "AI regulation" space is taken up with ex-ante regulatory proposals. All of the dominant approaches like the EU AI Act include some variation of getting experts to "audit" the weights for "bias", and risks, etc. and approve the models before release (which imposes costs only large corporations can pay) or outright caps/bans based on model size or specific capabilities. There's precious little active interest among regulators towards ex-post regulation, like statutory tort liability (which wouldn't impose onerous requirements on OSS developers, only users).Note: there is decent academic work on ex-post regulatory approaches, but much, much less interest in ex-post stuff among those in the pro-regulatory community with influence.reply

> Or you could just impose tort liability for individuals who misuse modelsWhich already exists and doesn't need new legislation.The reason why these "AI safety" firms are proposing regulations to kill local inference is because it creates a competitor to their models.  They want to find a way to pull off regulatory capture.And to be clear, what these people want to do is a free speech, potentially free press, violation.  They are trying to criminalize the LLM printing press all because they realize their moat can't survive competition.reply

I'm with you on the regulatory capture point. Some of the AI safety crew do actually seem to want regulatory capture leading to a small oligopoly of major labs (Dario would be one of them given his writing), but many of those in government and various external thinktanks are well-intentioned and don't seem to realize what they're advocating will lead to regulatory capture.>Which already exists and doesn't need new legislation.If there is clear intent, yes. The gap with existing operator and vicarious liability approaches is that they don't operate on strict liability; they don't fit well when you can't prove the operator intended a harmful result. This is a major gap with agents and to some extent a problem with complex AI more broadly. Decent number of academic papers on this.reply

> many of those in government and various external thinktanks are well-intentioned and don't seem to realize what they're advocating will lead to regulatory capture.There is a zero percent chance that anyone, in a regulatory body, advocating for banning OSS models doesn't realize it will lead to a moat (and regulatory capture) favoring the current big players.They may actually think the juice is worth the squeeze, but they know exactly what they're advocating for.reply

Maybe the actual people in the industry and academia but I've watched enough C-SPAN to know that we don't have the brightest bulbs in that room. And far too many of the ones who are smart enough are just bought off or promised cushy revolving door positions that they retire into.It really feels like we're in the declining imperial state that historians have written about for ages, about the internecine eunuch power struggles or the gradual fall of the Roman Empire. Rulers who rule for the sake of accruing power and influence only, heralding a feudal dark age where the warlords each carve out their respective limb from the imperial corpse.reply
It's no different from developers open sourcing a piece of code from their work eg Hadoop, in the hope that they can get future work on that software. Except it's not software it's regulations.reply

Did Hadoop have as much of an impact on a population level as, for eg, the regulation of tobacco? Or banks? Would it have been impossible for us to reach our current state of the world without it? And is the world better for it?Irrespective of that golden goose, how many other examples are there of the shoe being on the other foot, where the small guy wins out? Because I know maybe one SWE out of hundreds that made it big doing their own thing. Meanwhile legislators and the revolving door to lobbying and cushy positions is as normal a practice as Agile is - everyone does some form of it, many poorly, but its standard for that industry.reply
I'm just drawing an analogy not adding a value judgment. Stop ranting. Everyone knows that regulations are imposed and most of the time software is not.reply

And what was the purpose of the analogy? I'm responding to an embedded value statement where you normalize something that is eroding civil society by painting it as something as innocuous as a solo dev cashing out. If that wasn't your intent then I'm having trouble understanding why you even needed to make that analogy.reply

title: New material gets stronger the more it bends (washu.edu)
comments: "Work Hardening", such as with Manganese steel, AKA Hadfield steel or mangalloy used in armor.reply

That has nothing to do with the article.> The patented polymer, created in Ke’s lab with compatibility for 3D printing, is made from a biodegradable blend of sugar crystals and polyethylene glycol, a compound often used in laxatives and other health products. The mixture forms a hydrogel, a flexible material that can absorb and retain large amounts of water.reply

But it does. It's not the same mechanism, but it's a similar result.Though work hardening happens with many other metals, not only those special ones. It's just that normally it results in brittleness. Manganese steel is special in that it stays tough.reply

True.Also some ordinary plastic materials (I think polystyrene might be among those) harden if you flex them repeatedly, but when they harden they also become very brittle, so you can break them very easily.If you have a stick of such a plastic, it is easy to notice this behavior, because in the beginning you can flex the stick easily, but after a few times it becomes much harder to flex, but if at that time you continue flexing it, it breaks immediately.reply
how do you evaluate material strength without stressing it?reply

I hate metallurgy discussions among novices.“STRONGER” is a term that means nothing to me anymore. Stronger is a direction… what chart though?New material gets gains tensile strength and comes more brittle the more it bends. Not quite the same feel.reply

I would generally agree about terminology, but this article is about a polymer hydrogel that has a deformation strengthening mechanism, which seems pretty cool! Not the same mechanism as in metals, it’s something about aromatic rings that couple together during  deformation? I don’t have full text but the abstract says it improves tensile strength, modulus, and fracture toughness which is also pretty different from work hardening behaviorhttps://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02795-0reply

I'm a novice, but I had the same complaint. Stronger... like glass? Or like copper? Or wood? Concrete?Gaining tensile strength and losing toughness makes sense to me, thanks. EDIT: except it sounds like that's wrong; for this hydrogel, fracture energy goes up so it gets tougher, not more brittle.reply
Wanna explain the right terms to use so that us novices can improve?reply
Paper is linked in tfa: "Mechanical training enhances Young's modulus, tensile strength, fracture energy and fatigue threshold by up to an order of magnitude"reply
first_paragraph: The Source								Most materials get weaker with use. But a team led by Chenfeng Ke, a professor of chemistry in Arts & Sciences at Washington University in St. Louis, has created a polymer that defies the usual laws of wear and tear. “Our smart material actually gets stronger the more it’s bent and strained,” Ke said. “It has properties we have never seen before. It can remember, adapt, learn and grow. We’re excited to think about the possible applications.”The breakthrough was described in a study published online in Nature Materials. title: Per Arm's request, this site will be discontinued on 4 December 2026 :( (jonpalmisc.com)
comments: Hi, didn't expect to see this here, so adding a bit of info:They are requesting removal stating that I am using their trademarks and IP by hosting their documentation, which seems hard to work around while still keeping the site useful.People have contacted me offering to host mirrors, or suggesting I lawyer up or release the source code (sans Arm IP) to generate the same site for personal use. I'll be looking into all of these options.For those unfamiliar with this site until now: it's the ISA documentation, but with search and without all the popups and bloat. The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily.Thanks for the support, everyone! :)reply

Thanks for hosting this for so long.  I say this in jest (because it's not functionally filling the same need), but if you wanted to host https://riscv.jonpalmisc.com/ none of us in the RISC-V community would be upset at all. :grin:reply

Have you contacted their lawyers asking if they would be willing to license some use of the trademarks and/or IP? It's likely that the person sending this has the job of taking down infringing content, but that a higher level lawyer would permit it with a license agreement in place. Even if they only request $1 a year or something small, the goal wouldn't be a fee but to establish that everyone agrees it's their property being used with their permission.reply

Chances are ARM outsources this stuff to faceless third parties who don’t care. Hopefully someone in ARM sees this here and thinks it’s very positive rather than bad for them and something can be worked out!reply
If it would be useful to you in any way, even tangentially, you can email us for a free-forever account.reply
Can confirm, even after having paid substantially more than free for my forever rsync.net account, useful doesn't even begin to describe it. This offer would totally make me feel better.reply
Somewhat ironic that Arm is also listed as one of the headline customers on your landing page.reply

If you're using the $X trademarks to refer to genuine $X products, as opposed to your own knockoffs, then you don't need a licence, or at least that's how it usually works with trademarks in a sane jurisdiction. I don't know about the other "IP". Perhaps you could ask for clarification.reply
Right -- you're referring to "nominative fair use" of trademarks.  However, I suspect this is actually about copyright of the docs, not trademark of the ARM marks.reply

Not being too familiar with the content, would it be feasible to ship an open source project that is just a pass thru site that transforms their annoying popup-bloated site into something more like yours, but pulls from their source material and doesn’t strip the copyright?
